headline: Russia blacks out 550,000 Ukrainian homes as Kyiv says the US gave no warning; China starts policing AI and solar tech exports; Lavrov courts Tehran on Hormuz; prosecutors tie the OpenAI bugging suspect to Saudi backers; and Anthropic's share fund draws a SpaceX-for-every-kid reply from Musk.

stories.title: Russia knocks out power to 550,000 Ukrainian homes, and Kyiv says the US gave no early warning
facts: Overnight wave: 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and region plus 200+ drones; more than 10 energy facilities hit (Zelensky, Reuters).
At least 550,000 households lost power, heat or water; outages in 10 regions per grid operator Ukrenergo; at least four killed across Ukraine.
Air force: no warning before the first ~23:00 strike on Kyiv power plants, a warning only for the later 03:00 wave.
Zelensky says some US deliveries are delayed at Pentagon level while Russia gets sanctions relief; Rubio denies any pause in intelligence sharing.
stories.whyItMatters: Coming right after Washington suspended Russia sanctions, the missing warnings feed Kyiv's fear that intelligence is being used as leverage — with winter and Patriot shortages making grid attacks far more damaging.

stories.title: China moves to restrict exports of AI, solar-manufacturing and biotech know-how
facts: Draft from the commerce ministry and others lists 40 technologies: 26 would need export licences, 14 would be banned outright (Reuters via heise).
23 of them are AI techniques, including AI agents and methods for large models; app/web access and already-public AI stay allowed.
Also covered: solar-cell production processes (equipment, not finished modules) and cell and gene therapy methods.
Comments are open until Nov 15, but a registration duty for transferring these technologies has applied since Friday.
stories.whyItMatters: This turns last week's draft into a live regime — Beijing is now using its lead in solar equipment and open models as export leverage, which matters for any European firm relying on Chinese tech transfer.

stories.title: Lavrov flies from the Gulf to Tehran, pitching Moscow as mediator to stop a return to full-scale war
facts: First Lavrov visit to Iran since February 2025; met FM Araghchi, with President Pezeshkian later on Monday.
A day earlier in Bahrain, GCC states urged Moscow to press Tehran to halt attacks and reopen Hormuz shipping; GCC counts 7,000+ Iranian missiles and drones since the war began.
Lavrov tied restored navigation to protection for Iran against renewed attacks and said Russian staff will gradually return to the Bushehr nuclear plant.
Araghchi blamed Hormuz insecurity on US and Israeli aggression and said regional problems have "no military solution".
stories.whyItMatters: With US–Iran talks stalled and Brent hovering near $110, Moscow is positioning itself as the broker on Hormuz — while it simultaneously gets sanctions relief from Washington on Ukraine.

image.alt: Sergey Lavrov meets Abbas Araghchi in Tehran

stories.title: Prosecutors: ex-OpenAI engineer accused of bugging an exec room had "considerable" Saudi support
facts: Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly hid an audio recorder behind a TV in an OpenAI conference room; OpenAI found it Sept 30, the FBI arrested him Oct 9.
Filing says he was in frequent WhatsApp contact with an unnamed Saudi royal who tried to recruit him for a Saudi AI initiative ("Saudi needs you more then the US!").
A Saudi military official allegedly paid his wife and son's one-way business-class flight out the day after his arrest.
Prosecutors say OpenAI executives met government officials in that room; they want him held. Defense says the Riyadh ticket was booked Sept 13 and offers GPS monitoring and a bond.
stories.whyItMatters: It's the clearest case yet of state-linked espionage risk inside a frontier lab — and lands while OpenAI is already fighting an ex-employee over files taken to Apple.

image.alt: BBC illustration for the OpenAI recording-device case

stories.title: Anthropic commits 5% of its shares to a public-benefit fund; Musk answers with a SpaceX share for every US kid
facts: Anthropic (Sun): 5% of shares to a new Public Benefit Fund LLC, subject to stockholder approval, plus 2% more for every 50% rise in value above a baseline.
Fund may make large donations or direct distributions, e.g. on AI labor-market impacts; no lobbying or political giving. Anthropic says ~20% of its shares are now pledged to the public good overall.
Musk replied "give the shares directly to the public", then pledged one of his SpaceX shares to "every kid in America" next year, "the first of many".
At Friday's $146.03 close and ~72–73m US children that is roughly $10.5bn; no details on eligibility or mechanics. SpaceX reports earnings Tuesday.
stories.whyItMatters: Equity-for-the-public is turning into a new front in the AI rivalry — and Musk's pledge could mint tens of millions of retail SpaceX holders right before its first big earnings print.

image.alt: Anthropic: Investing in the public benefit

stories.title: DAX closes 1.2% lower; VW reportedly orders pay freeze to 2030 while DHL lifts its outlook
facts: DAX ended about 1.2% (~300 pts) lower at ~25,320, with Rheinmetall the biggest loser and the France unrest weighing on European markets (Handelsblatt).
VW works council and IG Metall: management told HR worldwide to plan zero pay rises until 2030 for 660,000+ staff, effective since early October; VW won't comment on "speculation".
IG Metall warns of ≥10% real-wage loss; contract talks start late November, with the union demanding 5%.
DHL raised its 2026 group EBIT goal to over €7.0bn (from >€6.5bn) after Q3 EBIT rose ~16% to ~€1.71bn, yet the stock slipped on profit-taking.
stories.whyItMatters: VW's freeze, on top of 50,000 planned job cuts, sets up the hardest German auto wage round in years — just as the government courts investors at this week's Invest in Germany summit.
